Settings read out of the environment, typed, and reported all at once.

Three things, and the third is the one worth having:

- **Typed.** `int("PORT")` gives an `Int` or says why it could not.
- **Redacted.** `secret("DB_PASSWORD")` gives a `Redacted<String>`, which
  cannot reach a log line or a JSON body -- see `std::core::Redacted`.
- **Collected.** Every reader answers `Validated`, so `map2` reports *every*
  missing key in one pass. The alternative is a person starting the service
  five times to be told five things it knew the first time.

```khora
derive(Show)
type Settings = { host: String, port: Int };

fn settings() -> Validated<Settings, ConfigError> with { env: Env } {
  Validated::map2(
    or_default(string("HOST"), "0.0.0.0"),
    int("PORT"),
    fn (host, port) => { host: host, port: port },
  )
}
```

### Why there is no `Config<A>` description type

The obvious port of this idea from a language with no effect rows is a
*description*: a value denoting "read PORT as an integer", interpreted
later by a provider, so that a test can swap the provider. The description
layer exists entirely to defer the read.

**Khora's provider is the `Env` handler, and it is already swappable.** A
test writes `with { env: handler for Env { .. } }` and these functions read
from it, because the row says they read from something. So the description
is ceremony: an AST, an interpreter for it, and a second way to spell every
reader. What that layer bought -- typed parsing, composition, and error
accumulation -- is bought here by the return type instead.

### Why nothing here raises

`Env::variable` raises `EnvError` when the manifest does not grant a name,
and every reader here catches it into `ConfigError::Denied`. Reading
configuration is the one place where "tell me everything that is wrong" is
the whole job, and a `raises` would stop at the first one -- which is
exactly the behaviour this module exists to avoid. A denial is a
configuration problem like any other, and it belongs in the same list.

## Types

### ConfigError

```khora
derive(Eq, Show)
pub type ConfigError =
  | Missing(name: String)
  | Malformed(name: String, wanted: String, found: String)
  | Denied(name: String);
```

Why a setting could not be read.

**Three cases, because they are three different jobs.** `Missing` is
somebody's deployment script; `Malformed` is a typo in a value; `Denied` is
a line in `khora.toml`. Collapsing them would send a reader to the wrong
file, which is the failure `IoError::Denied` and `EnvError::Denied` were
both added to avoid.

## Functions

### report

```khora
pub fn report(errors: List<ConfigError>) -> String
```

Every reason, one per line, in the order they were read.

What a service prints just before it stops, and the reason the whole module
answers `Validated`: this list is allowed to have more than one thing in it.

### string

```khora
pub fn string(name: String) -> Validated<String, ConfigError> with { env: Env }
```

The variable's text, or why not.

Every other reader is this one plus a parse, so the denial is caught in one
place and the shape of the answer is decided in one place.

### int

```khora
pub fn int(name: String) -> Validated<Int, ConfigError> with { env: Env }
```

The variable as a whole number.

### decimal

```khora
pub fn decimal(name: String) -> Validated<Decimal, ConfigError> with { env: Env }
```

The variable as an exact decimal.

**This is the language for money and the config reader could not read
any.** A rate, a threshold, a fee cap and a currency amount are all
settings, and the three readers above are `Int`, `Bool` and `String` --
so the only way to configure a rate was to read it as text and parse it
again at the call site, or worse, to read it as an `Int` of basis points
and hope everybody downstream remembered the scale.

Exponent notation is refused, the way `Decimal::of_string` refuses it: a
number arriving as `1e-3` has been through a float somewhere, and a
configuration file is exactly where that would go unnoticed.

**The scale is whatever was written.** `0.10` reads at two places and
`0.1` at one, and they are the same number -- `Decimal`'s `Eq` says so --
but a rate written to four places stays written to four, which is what
makes a total built from it print the way the person who set it expected.

### bool

```khora
pub fn bool(name: String) -> Validated<Bool, ConfigError> with { env: Env }
```

The variable as a flag.

**`true`/`false`/`1`/`0`, and nothing else is a guess.** `yes`, `on`, `Y`
and an empty string all mean "true" somewhere, and a config reader that
accepts every one of them accepts a typo as a `false`. This one says so
instead.

### secret

```khora
pub fn secret(name: String) -> Validated<Redacted<String>, ConfigError> with { env: Env }
```

The variable, wrapped so it cannot be printed.

The one every password and API key should go through. What comes back has
no `Encode` and shows as `<redacted>`, so a record holding it stays
printable and serialisable-refusing -- `std::core::Redacted` has the whole
argument.

### or_default

```khora
pub fn or_default<A>(inner: Validated<A, ConfigError>, fallback: A) -> Validated<A, ConfigError>
```

A fallback for a setting nobody set.

**Fires on `Missing` and on nothing else.** A value that is present and
wrong must still fail: `PORT=eigthy` silently becoming `80` is the bug this
module is for, and it is the one a fallback written the obvious way
introduces. The distinction is only available because the error is
structured rather than a string.
